nameStory: The Driftwood Rim-lichen gets its name from its love of weathered wood, especially the kind of sun-bleached, salt-worn driftwood you might find along New England's rocky shores. Like many rim lichens, it forms distinctive disc-shaped fruiting bodies with raised edges that look like tiny bowls or rims. The species name 'xylophila' literally means 'wood-loving' in Latin, perfectly capturing this lichen's preferred home.
description: Driftwood Rim-lichen is a crusty, flat-growing lichen that forms thin patches on weathered wood surfaces. It creates a grayish or whitish coating that can look almost painted on, with small disc-shaped structures dotting the surface like tiny buttons. These discs, called apothecia, are the lichen's reproductive structures and often have darker centers surrounded by pale rims. Individual patches can spread several inches across on suitable wood surfaces.

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Found exclusively on weathered wood, especially driftwood, old fence posts, and sun-bleached wooden structures near water

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms a thin, crusty coating that feels slightly rough and chalky to the touch, like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale gray to whitish when dry, may appear slightly darker and more defined when damp

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Small disc-shaped apothecia with darker centers and pale raised rims, scattered across the surface like tiny embedded coins

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Thin and closely attached to the wood surface, with a slightly powdery or granular feel when rubbed gently

habitat: Look for Driftwood Rim-lichen on weathered wooden surfaces throughout New England, especially near coastal areas, lakes, and rivers. It particularly favors driftwood, old dock pilings, weathered fence posts, and abandoned wooden structures that have been exposed to sun and moisture cycles. The wood must be well-aged and weathered, as this lichen rarely colonizes fresh lumber.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more visible as spring moisture activates growth, with colors appearing more vivid and defined against the damp wood.
seasonality.summer: Most easily spotted during dry summer conditions when the pale coloration contrasts sharply with darkened, weathered wood surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Reproductive discs may be most prominent in fall, appearing as small dark spots with pale rims across the lichen's surface.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but may appear more muted; look for it on south-facing wooden surfaces that catch winter sunlight.

funFact: This lichen is essentially a solar-powered wood preservative - it actually helps protect the weathered wood it lives on from further decay by forming a protective coating that slows water penetration and UV damage.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other pale rim lichens growing on wood, but the exclusive preference for weathered wood (rather than bark or rock) is the key distinguishing feature. Remember: if it's on driftwood or old wooden structures, you're likely looking at the right species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting coastal driftwood, this lichen can be found on any type of weathered wood throughout New England, including inland areas where old wooden structures provide suitable habitat.
compareHints: Unlike its rim lichen relatives that prefer rock or bark, Driftwood Rim-lichen is uniquely specialized for weathered wood substrates. Common Rim Lichen typically grows on rocks and has more pronounced raised rims, while Granite-speck Rim Lichen is found exclusively on granite surfaces. The wood-only habitat makes this species relatively easy to distinguish from its genus-mates.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pink-eyed White-rim stands out from its Lecanora relatives by its distinctive pink to reddish-brown apothecia with white rims - most other rim lichens in the genus have brown, black, or yellow reproductive discs.
Among the rim lichens in its genus, Mapledust Lichen stands out for its distinctly dusty, powdery surface texture.
Among its rim-lichen relatives, Mealy Rim-lichen is distinguished by its distinctly granular, powdery surface texture.
Among its rim lichen relatives, Bumpy Rim-lichen stands out for having the most prominently raised fruiting bodies - they truly stick up from the surface rather than sitting flush with it.

Frosted Rim-lichen stands out from its Lecanora relatives by maintaining a consistently pale, whitish color rather than the grayer tones of Common Rim Lichen or the more yellowish hues of some other species in the genus.
